title: BY HIS STRIPES WE ARE HEALED… SO WHY ARE SOME FAITHFUL CHRISTIANS STILL DYING SICK?
paragraphs: BY HIS STRIPES WE ARE HEALED… SO WHY ARE SOME FAITHFUL CHRISTIANS STILL DYING SICK?

The heartbreaking truth about Isaiah 53:5 that challenges the prosperity gospel, confronts our deepest disappointments, and reveals a Savior whose wounds promise something even greater than the miracle we are begging Him to perform.
She prayed until her voice was almost gone.
The Bible lay open beside the hospital bed. Her husband's breathing had become shallow. Machines whispered and beeped in a room where every second felt like an eternity.
She had fasted. She had believed. She had asked the elders to pray. She had anointed him with oil. She had declared the promises of Scripture over his body.
And through tears she whispered the verse she had heard preached a thousand times.
“By His stripes we are healed.”
But the cancer kept spreading.
And one night, despite every prayer, every tear, every desperate declaration of faith…
Her husband died.
What happened to the promise?
Was her faith too weak?
Had she prayed incorrectly?
Was there some hidden sin that prevented the miracle?
Or had she misunderstood what God was promising in the first place?
Perhaps you have never stood beside a hospital bed like hers.

But maybe you have watched your mother suffer. Maybe your child has a diagnosis that makes you afraid to answer the telephone. Maybe your body has been fighting a disease for years while people keep telling you to believe harder.
And somewhere beneath your worship songs and your Sunday smiles, there is a question you are almost ashamed to ask.
If Jesus was wounded for my healing, why am I still hurting?
Please don't rush past that question.
Because the answer is not found in pretending that suffering isn't real.
And it certainly isn't found in accusing wounded Christians of lacking faith.
The answer begins at a cross, where the Son of God suffered wounds He did not deserve to accomplish a redemption we could never earn.
And understanding what those wounds actually purchased may change the way you pray, suffer, hope, and follow Jesus for the rest of your life.
The prophet Isaiah wrote approximately seven centuries before the earthly ministry of Jesus Christ:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” — Isaiah 53:5, KJV
These are among the most beautiful words ever written about the suffering Messiah.
But beautiful words can become dangerous when we separate them from their intended meaning.
The Hebrew phrase behind “and with his stripes we are healed” is:
וּבַחֲבֻרָתוֹ נִרְפָּא־לָנוּ
Uvaḥavurato nirpa lanu.
A careful translation is, “And by his wound, healing has come to us,” or, more traditionally, “And with his stripes we are healed.”
The Hebrew word חֲבֻרָה (ḥavurah) refers to a wound or stripe, particularly the injury produced by a blow.
The verb רָפָא (rapha) means “to heal.” It can describe physical healing, but Scripture also uses healing language for spiritual and covenant restoration.
That distinction matters enormously.
The Hebrew word itself does not automatically prove that Isaiah was promising immediate bodily recovery to every believer.
We must allow the surrounding passage to explain the kind of healing Isaiah is emphasizing.
And what surrounds this famous promise?
Transgressions.
Iniquities.
Punishment.
Peace.
Sin.
Isaiah 53:6 continues:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
The deepest wound addressed in this passage is humanity's rebellion against God.
The Servant suffers because we have sinned.
He is wounded because we have wandered.
He bears judgment so that guilty people can receive peace.
Isaiah is describing the astonishing exchange at the heart of the Gospel.
The righteous One suffers for the unrighteous.
The innocent One bears the burden of the guilty.
The Holy One makes a way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
And the healing Isaiah celebrates is inseparable from that saving work.
This does not mean God is uninterested in your physical suffering.
It means we must not reduce the cross to a guarantee that Christians will never remain sick.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make dying people temporarily healthy.
He came to save sinners, conquer death, and bring His redeemed people into everlasting life.
And here is where the story becomes even more extraordinary.
Centuries after Isaiah wrote those words, the apostle Peter quoted the same prophecy.
But notice what he said immediately afterward.
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.” — 1 Peter 2:24, KJV
The Greek phrase is:
οὗ τῷ μώλωπι ἰάθητε
Hou tō mōlōpi iathēte.
Literally, “By whose wound you were healed.”
The word μώλωψ (mōlōps) refers to a bruise, welt, or wound.
The verb ἰάθητε (iathēte) means “you were healed.”
But Peter does something that should make every serious Bible reader stop.
He explains the purpose of Christ bearing our sins: that we might die to sins and live to righteousness.
Then he continues:
“For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.” — 1 Peter 2:25, KJV
Do you see it?
Peter does not say, “You were physically sick, but now none of you can remain sick.”
He says you were wandering sheep, but now you have returned to your Shepherd.
The healing in Peter's immediate explanation concerns our restoration from sin and estrangement from God.
The cross brings forgiveness, reconciliation, and a transformed life.
That is not a lesser miracle.
That is the miracle upon which every other Christian hope depends.
A healed body can still die.
A forgiven sinner who belongs to Jesus has eternal life.
And yet we must be careful not to swing into the opposite error.
Because the Bible does not teach that physical healing is irrelevant to Christ's mission.
Matthew 8:16–17 records Jesus casting out spirits and healing the sick, then explicitly connects those healings to Isaiah's prophecy:
“That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses.” — Matthew 8:17, KJV
This is crucial.
Matthew shows that Jesus' healing ministry truly belongs to the fulfillment of Isaiah's vision.
His compassion was not symbolic.
Blind eyes opened.
Paralyzed people walked.
Lepers were cleansed.
People with genuine physical illnesses experienced genuine physical restoration.
Jesus cared about suffering bodies.
He still does.
So the biblical question is not whether Christ's redemptive mission includes physical healing.
It does.
The question is whether every believer is promised complete physical healing right now, in this present life, whenever healing is requested in faith.
And Scripture does not establish that guarantee.
The kingdom of God has already broken into history through Jesus Christ.
But its final consummation has not yet arrived.
Christ has risen.
Death has been defeated decisively.
Yet believers still experience weakness, disease, aging, grief, and physical death.
We live between the victory already accomplished and the restoration still awaiting its fullness.
Romans 8:23 says that believers, even though they have the firstfruits of the Spirit, still groan inwardly while awaiting “the redemption of our body.”
Read that again.
Believers who possess the Holy Spirit are still waiting for the redemption of their bodies.
Paul was not describing Christians who lacked sufficient faith.
He was describing the normal tension of Christian existence before the resurrection.
We have received salvation in Christ.
We are being sanctified by His Spirit.
And we await the day when our bodies will be raised imperishable.
That future is not uncertain.
But the timing matters.
The final, complete healing of God's people is guaranteed through Christ.
Complete freedom from every illness before death is not.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable evidence comes from a man who personally witnessed extraordinary miracles.
The apostle Paul.
Paul preached Christ.
Paul healed the sick by God's power.
Paul witnessed supernatural deliverance.
Yet Paul also carried an affliction he desperately wanted removed.
He called it a thorn in the flesh.
We are not told precisely what that thorn was, so we should not confidently diagnose it as a particular disease.
But we know it caused real distress.
Paul pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart from him.
And God's answer was not the answer Paul requested.
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Imagine that.
The apostle who preached the power of the risen Christ received an answer that did not involve the removal of his affliction.
Not because Christ lacked power.
Not because grace had failed.
Not because Paul needed to discover a more effective declaration.
But because God's sufficient grace and Christ's sustaining power were being displayed in weakness.
Sometimes God glorifies Himself by removing suffering.
Sometimes He glorifies Himself by sustaining His children through suffering.
Neither reality gives us permission to treat illness as proof of spiritual failure.
And Paul was not the only faithful believer who experienced bodily weakness.
In Philippians 2:25–27, Epaphroditus became gravely ill, nearly to the point of death.
Paul did not accuse him of unbelief.
He recognized that God had shown him mercy.
In 1 Timothy 5:23, Paul advised Timothy to use a little wine for his stomach and his frequent ailments.
He did not tell Timothy that recurring illness was impossible for a genuine Christian.
In 2 Timothy 4:20, Paul wrote that he had left Trophimus sick at Miletus.
These passages do not deny divine healing.
They dismantle the idea that faithful Christians are guaranteed uninterrupted physical health.
Even devoted servants of Christ experienced sickness.
And the Bible does not portray their suffering as evidence that Jesus had abandoned them.
Think about what that means for the woman beside the hospital bed.
Think about what it means for the father watching his child undergo another treatment.
Think about what it means for the believer whose prayers have not produced the miracle everyone expected.
Your illness is not a verdict on the strength of your faith.
Your unanswered request is not proof that Jesus has stopped loving you.
Your suffering does not automatically mean that you are being punished for a hidden sin.
Jesus directly challenged that assumption in John 9:1–3 when His disciples asked whether a man's blindness resulted from his sin or his parents' sin.
Christ rejected their proposed explanation.
Not every sickness can be traced to a particular personal wrongdoing.
Yes, Scripture teaches that sin and death entered the human story through the fall.
Yes, particular sins can sometimes have physical consequences.
But it is biblically irresponsible to assume that every sick Christian is sick because of unbelief, disobedience, or a secret offense.
And it is cruel to turn that assumption into a burden for people who are already suffering.
A mother who has buried her child does not need a preacher suggesting that she failed to believe hard enough.
A cancer patient does not need someone telling him that chemotherapy proves he has abandoned faith.
A disabled believer does not need to be treated as a defective testimony.
They need the truth.
They need compassion.
They need the presence of the body of Christ.
They need the Gospel.
And they need to know that the Savior who suffered on the cross understands suffering from the inside.
Jesus did not stand at a safe distance from human pain.
He entered it.
He wept at Lazarus's tomb.
He experienced exhaustion.
He endured betrayal.
He was beaten, mocked, scourged, and crucified.
He knows what it means to cry out in anguish.
And in Gethsemane, Jesus prayed that the cup might pass from Him, while surrendering Himself to the Father's will.
His prayer was not an expression of unbelief.
It was perfect trust expressed in the presence of terrible suffering.
This matters because some Christians have been taught that saying “Your will be done” is a confession of weak faith.
But Jesus Himself prayed in submission to the Father's will.
If surrender were unbelief, the sinless Son of God would have been guilty of it.
He was not.
Biblical faith does not mean commanding God to obey our preferred outcome.
Biblical faith means trusting God's character even when we cannot understand His providence.
We may pray boldly for healing.
We should pray boldly for healing.
James 5:14–16 encourages the sick to call for the elders of the church, to receive prayer and anointing with oil in the name of the Lord.
We should not explain away that invitation.
God hears prayer.
God can heal.
God sometimes heals in remarkable and unexpected ways.
And when He does, we should give Him glory.
But James's instruction must be read alongside the rest of Scripture, not turned into a mechanical formula that forces every prayer to produce an immediate cure.
The same Bible that calls us to pray for healing also records faithful believers who remained afflicted.
God's promises do not contradict one another.
Our interpretations must make room for everything He has revealed.
And seeking medical treatment is not a betrayal of Christian faith.
Medicine, surgery, therapy, and responsible medical care can be received with gratitude as ordinary means through which God may preserve life and relieve suffering.
Prayer and medical treatment are not enemies.
Do not stop necessary treatment because someone has convinced you that genuine faith requires refusing it.
The God who can heal miraculously is not dishonored when His people seek wise medical help.
But perhaps your struggle goes deeper than theology.
Perhaps you have already accepted that healing is not guaranteed.
And still…
You are disappointed.
You believed God could heal your father.
He died.
You begged God to restore your marriage.
It collapsed.
You prayed for your child's suffering to end.
The suffering continued.
And now every time someone says, “God is good,” something inside you quietly asks:
Then why did He let this happen?
That question is painful.
But Scripture gives us language for grief rather than demanding that we pretend.
The Psalms contain cries of confusion, sorrow, abandonment, and desperate longing.
The Bible does not erase lament from the vocabulary of faith.
Even the Lord Jesus wept.
And this is where we must distinguish between what God has promised and what we desperately wish He had promised.
God has not promised that following Jesus will protect us from every tragedy.
Jesus told His disciples:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” — John 16:33, KJV
Notice what He did not say.
He did not say there would be no tribulation.
He said He had overcome the world.
Our confidence is not that suffering will never touch us.
Our confidence is that suffering will not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And that brings us to a scene more powerful than any hospital miracle we could imagine.
A cemetery.
A grave.
A grieving family.
A man who had been dead four days.
When Jesus arrived at the tomb of Lazarus, Martha spoke words that have echoed through generations of disappointed believers.
“Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.” — John 11:21, KJV
Can you hear the grief beneath that sentence?
Lord, You could have stopped this.
Lord, You had the power.
Lord, why didn't You come sooner?
Maybe you have never spoken those exact words.
But perhaps you have prayed their meaning.
Jesus did not respond by mocking Martha's grief.
He gave her a revelation.
“I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.” — John 11:25, KJV
Not merely, “I can prevent death.”
Not merely, “I can heal disease.”
I am the resurrection and the life.
Jesus was revealing something greater than temporary rescue from physical suffering.
He was revealing His authority over death itself.
Then He called Lazarus from the grave.
The dead man came out alive.
What a miracle.
But remember something easily overlooked.
Lazarus eventually died again.
His resurrection to mortal life was a glorious sign, not the final resurrection promised to all God's redeemed people.
The ultimate hope of Christianity is not an endless series of temporary recoveries in bodies that remain subject to death.
It is the resurrection of the dead through Jesus Christ.
It is the defeat of death itself.
It is a new creation in which God's people will no longer be subject to the corruption that now fills hospitals, funeral homes, and cemeteries.
Revelation 21:4 declares:
“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.”
That is the promise.
Not that every Christian will escape the hospital.
Not that every cancer will disappear before the funeral.
Not that every faithful prayer will result in the physical outcome we desire.
But that in Christ, death itself will be abolished.
Pain will not merely be managed.
It will be gone.
Grief will not merely become easier to carry.
Its causes will be removed.
The redeemed will not merely receive another temporary extension of mortal life.
They will share in resurrection life.
And this hope is secure because Jesus Christ truly rose from the dead.
Christianity is not built on the claim that believers never suffer.
It is built on the crucified and risen Savior who conquered the grave.
That is why the resurrection matters so profoundly.
Without it, the cross would be remembered as another terrible execution.
But because Christ rose, His sacrifice is vindicated, His promises are trustworthy, and the future resurrection of His people is certain.
First Corinthians 15 anchors our hope in that victory.
The final enemy to be destroyed is death.
And death will not survive the reign of Jesus Christ.
So when we say, “By His stripes we are healed,” we must say it with the fullness of biblical truth.
Through Christ's suffering, sinners can be forgiven and reconciled to God.
His kingdom brings genuine healing and restoration, including physical healings that testify to His power and compassion.
And through His death and resurrection, everyone who belongs to Him has the certain hope of complete bodily redemption when He returns.
But we must not promise every suffering Christian an immediate physical cure that Scripture does not guarantee.
The cross is too glorious to be reduced to a slogan.
The Gospel is too precious to be twisted into a transaction.
And the wounded are too precious to be crushed by false expectations.
Perhaps someone once told you that if you remained sick, you simply did not believe enough.
Perhaps you repeated positive declarations while your condition worsened.
Perhaps you secretly wondered whether God was disappointed in you.
Hear this carefully.
Jesus did not bleed on Calvary so that His suffering children could be condemned by people who misunderstand His promises.
He bore our sins to bring us to God.
He rose from the dead to secure our hope.
And He calls us to trust Him, not because every earthly outcome will satisfy our expectations, but because He is faithful even when the road leads through suffering.
This truth does not make prayer unnecessary.
It makes prayer honest.
You can pray:
“Lord Jesus, please heal me.”
You can pray:
“Father, restore my child.”
You can pray:
“God, I believe You are able.”
And you can also pray:
“Lord, even if the answer is not what I want, keep me close to You. Give me grace to endure. Help me trust Your goodness.”
That is not surrendering to hopelessness.
That is surrendering to God.
And surrender is not the opposite of faith.
It is one of faith's deepest expressions.
But there is another danger we must confront.
Some people are so focused on receiving physical healing that they have never seriously considered their need for forgiveness.
They want Jesus to remove their pain.
But they do not want Him to confront their sin.
They want His miracles.
But they resist His lordship.
They want the benefits of the cross without surrendering to the crucified King.
And that is a tragedy greater than any illness.
Because the greatest crisis of humanity is not merely that our bodies are dying.
It is that we have sinned against a holy God.
We have loved what He forbids.
We have neglected what He commands.
We have worshiped created things instead of the Creator.
We have tried to make ourselves righteous through religion, morality, or outward appearances.
But none of those things can erase our guilt.
That is why Jesus came.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And He calls sinners to repentance and faith.
Salvation is not purchased through religious performance, financial giving, or perfect health.
It is God's gift of grace received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakably clear.
You cannot buy forgiveness.
You cannot earn resurrection.
You need Jesus.
And when you truly come to Him, He does not merely offer you a better religious image.
He begins transforming your life.
He forgives.
He restores.
He teaches you to turn away from sin.
He gives you a new identity rooted in His grace.
And even when your circumstances remain painful, you can belong completely to Him.
That is what we mean when we say:
Not because every broken bone is instantly repaired.
Not because every diagnosis disappears.
Not because every earthly story ends with the miracle we wanted.

But because the greatest scandal in human history—the sinless Son of God condemned and crucified—became, according to God's saving purpose, the place where grace was displayed with breathtaking power.
The cross exposes the seriousness of our sin.
The resurrection announces the triumph of our Savior.
And the Gospel offers a future that suffering cannot destroy.
Maybe your body is still sick.
Maybe your loved one is still fighting.
Maybe you are grieving someone you begged God to spare.
You do not have to pretend that you are fine.
You do not have to manufacture a testimony that ends in physical recovery.
You do not have to hide your tears to prove that your faith is real.
Bring your grief to Jesus.
Bring your questions.
Bring your fear.
Bring the disappointment you have been afraid to admit.
And do not allow anyone to convince you that your suffering places you beyond the reach of His love.
Romans 8:38–39 reminds believers that neither death nor life, nor anything else in creation, can separate them from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Not the hospital.
Not the wheelchair.
Not the chemotherapy.
Not the unanswered question.
Not even the grave.
For those who belong to Christ, the grave is not the end of the story.
And one day, when the Lord Jesus returns, the promise of complete restoration will no longer be something we hold by faith while our bodies ache.
We will see the risen Christ.
And the people He has redeemed will be raised in glory.
Until then, we pray for healing without presuming to control God.
We seek medical help without shame.
We comfort the suffering without blaming them.
We grieve without surrendering our hope.
And we preach the Gospel without turning the wounds of Jesus into a promise He never made.
If this article has exposed something you have been carrying silently, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not need to explain your entire story publicly. Your pain is not something you owe the internet.
But your honest words may help another struggling believer realize that faith and tears can exist in the same heart.
Invite your family, your friends, those who have drifted from the faith, and those who are still searching for Jesus.
Because our mission is not to build an audience around personalities.
It is to keep pointing people toward the Savior.

For those who practice regular Christian giving, supporting faithful Gospel work can be a meaningful expression of generosity and stewardship. Scripture encourages cheerful, willing giving—not giving under guilt or pressure (2 Corinthians 9:7).
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, and faithful stewardship of what He has entrusted to you.
These are resources and gifts intended to encourage faith and keep biblical truth close in everyday life.
Those free resources are part of our desire to nourish believers with Scripture, not place spiritual growth behind a paywall.
Keep testing every teaching against Scripture.
Keep praying for the sick.
Keep caring for the wounded.
Keep sharing the hope of Jesus.
Because this ministry is not the source of your salvation.
Jesus Christ is.
It is whether you will entrust your life to the crucified and risen Savior.
If you have never truly turned to Christ, do not wait for a crisis to make you consider eternity.
Repent of your sins.
Believe the Gospel.
Come to Jesus.
He does not promise you a life without suffering.
He promises eternal life to those who believe in Him.
And if you already belong to Him, but your faith has been shaken by suffering, remember the truth that brought us here.
The wounds of Jesus are not proof that your life will never hurt.
They are proof of the astonishing price of your redemption.
And the empty tomb is the assurance that pain and death will not reign forever.
One day, the Christian who died trusting Jesus will stand alive before Him.
One day, the tears of God's redeemed people will be wiped away.
One day, the resurrection will answer the grave.
And until that day, even with trembling hands, aching bodies, and tear-filled eyes, we can cling to the One who was wounded for our transgressions and raised for our justification.
The stripes of Jesus do not guarantee that you will never enter a hospital bed—but His resurrection guarantees that, if you belong to Him, no grave will ever hold you forever.
